I learned most of this by screwing it up. Some of it I just thought through, and I’m still not sure about all of it.

Before making love, I want to know enough about the hard stuff that I’m not finding it all out after I’m bonded. Jealousy, attraction to other people, what happens under stress, old patterns, how recent the healing is, what each of us wants when things go bad, money. But asking, “How do you handle jealousy?” can get me a beautiful answer that tells me almost nothing. I’d rather ask what she thinks she would do in an actual situation.

Most of this I learned by getting it wrong. Some of it I figured out by thinking, and I’m still testing parts of it.

Before making love, I’d rather talk about the stuff that will be harder for me to hear once I’m attached. If she says she handles jealousy well, okay, but what does that mean when I’m attracted to somebody else? What does she do when she’s stressed? What old pattern still shows up? How recent is the healing? What does she want from me in a bad moment? What happens with money? I trust those answers more when we put an actual situation around them.

results.text:
Sex can speed the whole thing up enough by itself. I don’t want to also move in immediately and let that answer a bunch of questions I haven’t answered yet. Sometimes housing makes separate living unrealistic. Fine. But once we share a home, now there are practical reasons to stay even if one of us is having doubts. That’s why I like having a date on the calendar when we actually ask how it’s going instead of waiting for a crisis.

I also want some friends who know both of us. My old friends are going to be partial to me and hers to her. That isn’t a defect in the friendship. It just means I don’t want two separate cheering sections to be the only people around the relationship.

If we start having sex, I don’t want moving in to become the automatic next thing. Housing can make that difficult, but living together gives both people practical reasons not to reconsider the relationship. So if we do it, I’d rather decide in advance when we’re going to ask each other whether it’s actually working.

results.text:
I can know pretty quickly that I want to be with somebody. That tells me a lot less about whether I should raise children with her, share a house for twenty years, or build the rest of my life around her. A wonderful lover can still be a terrible long-term partner. One thing I try to catch is when “I’m taking a chance on this person” turns into “this is the right person” without any new evidence.

And being loved doesn’t mean I’m finished with my own inner practices. If I stop reparenting myself and regulating myself because she’s doing enough of it for me, I’ve made the relationship carry something it shouldn’t have to carry.

Wanting somebody romantically is one decision. Building a life with them is another. I might know the first one in a week. I cannot know in a week what she’ll be like as a co-parent or what years of ordinary life with her will feel like. So I watch for the moment “I’m taking a chance on this person” somehow becomes “this is the right person.” What happened between those two sentences?

I also keep doing my own practices. Being loved is wonderful, but it’s not evidence that I no longer need to know how to love and regulate myself.

results.text:
There’s also such a thing as talking too much. Ten profound conversations in one weekend can make me feel like I know someone when mostly I know what she says about herself. Then I need ordinary time. I need to see things I can’t get by asking better questions.

And if something feels off, I don’t have to decide that the feeling is true. I can just slow down long enough to find out what it was reacting to. That’s different from letting the chemistry tell me the feeling was stupid.
